questions.question: What is the main difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
questions.expected_answer: Plain EXPLAIN shows the planned query execution and estimates. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query and adds actual row counts and run times for plan nodes alongside the estimates.

answer_requirements.statement: Distinguish estimated plan information from actual execution measurements.
State explicitly that EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query.

span.text: It is possible to check the accuracy of the planner's estimates by using EXPLAIN's ANALYZE option. With this option, EXPLAIN actually executes the query, and then displays the true row counts and true run time accumulated within each plan node, along with the same estimates that a plain EXPLAIN shows.

questions.evidence_combination_note: E1 alone supports both the estimate-versus-measurement distinction and the fact that ANALYZE executes the query.

questions.question: Why are filters on the leading columns of a multicolumn B-tree index generally useful?
questions.expected_answer: Leading-column constraints make a multicolumn B-tree index efficient because leading equalities, together with an inequality on the first column without equality, limit the index range scanned. Conditions on later columns can still be checked in the index, but do not necessarily reduce that range. Missing a leading-column constraint does not categorically rule out index use.

answer_requirements.statement: Explain how leading equality constraints and the first inequality constraint limit the scanned range.
Avoid claiming that a later-column-only condition always prevents index use or always narrows the scanned range.

span.text: A multicolumn B-tree index can be used with query conditions that involve any subset of the index's columns, but the index is most efficient when there are constraints on the leading (leftmost) columns. The exact rule is that equality constraints on leading columns, plus any inequality constraints on the first column that does not have an equality constraint, will always be used to limit the portion of the index that is scanned. Constraints on columns to the right of these columns are checked in the index, so they'll always save visits to the table proper, but they do not necessarily reduce the portion of the index that has to be scanned.

questions.evidence_combination_note: E1 covers both leading-column efficiency and the limits of a blanket no-index-use rule for later columns.

questions.question: What relationship must the query condition have to a partial index predicate for the index to be usable?
questions.expected_answer: At planning time, PostgreSQL must recognize that the query's WHERE condition mathematically implies the partial-index predicate. Logical implication that the planner cannot recognize is insufficient; supported simple inequality implications or an appropriate matching predicate are examples. This establishes usability, not a guarantee that the planner will select the index.

answer_requirements.statement: State the direction of implication: query condition implies index predicate, with recognition at planning time.
Distinguish index usability from the planner choosing an index rather than a potentially cheaper path.

span.text: To be precise, a partial index can be used in a query only if the system can recognize that the WHERE condition of the query mathematically implies the predicate of the index. PostgreSQL does not have a sophisticated theorem prover that can recognize mathematically equivalent expressions that are written in different forms. (Not only is such a general theorem prover extremely difficult to create, it would probably be too slow to be of any real use.) The system can recognize simple inequality implications, for example “x < 1” implies “x < 2”; otherwise the predicate condition must exactly match part of the query's WHERE condition or the index will not be recognized as usable. Matching takes place at query planning time, not at run time.

Normally, PostgreSQL makes reasonable choices about index usage (e.g., it avoids them when retrieving common values, so the earlier example really only saves index size, it is not required to avoid index usage)

questions.evidence_combination_note: E1 supplies the predicate-implication and planning-time rule. E2 supports the selection qualification through the documented avoidance of indexes for common values; both are from the same source.

questions.question: Can a NULL replay_lag in pg_stat_replication be treated as zero seconds?
questions.expected_answer: No: a raw NULL replay_lag is not a measured numeric zero and should not automatically be interpreted as zero seconds. Lag can become NULL after a fully replayed standby is idle for a short time. A monitoring system may choose to display that state as missing data, zero, or the last known value, but that presentation policy does not make NULL itself a numeric measurement.

answer_requirements.statement: Do not identify a raw NULL lag with a measured numeric zero.
Explain that NULL can occur on a fully caught-up, idle standby.

span.text: If the standby server has entirely caught up with the sending server and there is no more WAL activity, the most recently measured lag times will continue to be displayed for a short time and then show NULL.

In particular, when the standby has caught up completely, pg_stat_replication shows the time taken to write, flush and replay the most recent reported WAL location rather than zero as some users might expect. This is consistent with the goal of measuring synchronous commit and transaction visibility delays for recent write transactions. To reduce confusion for users expecting a different model of lag, the lag columns revert to NULL after a short time on a fully replayed idle system. Monitoring systems should choose whether to represent this as missing data, zero or continue to display the last known value.

questions.evidence_combination_note: E2 alone supports a complete answer. E1 is an alternative supporting passage for the idle, caught-up case; retrieving both chunks is not mandatory.
scope_notes: NULL alone is not proof of a replication failure. The source explicitly permits a monitoring presentation policy; do not turn the reference answer into a claim that a dashboard can never display zero.

optional_guidance.statement: Distinguish the database value from a monitoring presentation policy that may choose missing data, zero, or the last known value.

questions.question: With an index on (customer_id, created_at), does filtering only on created_at always require a Seq Scan, and how can we inspect the chosen path?
questions.expected_answer: No. For a multicolumn B-tree index in PostgreSQL 18, filtering only on the second column does not automatically force a Seq Scan. Skip scan may be useful, for example when the leading column has few distinct values and repeated index searches are estimated to be cheaper. It is not guaranteed; data distribution and estimated costs affect the choice. Use EXPLAIN on the actual query to inspect the chosen plan.

answer_requirements.statement: Reject the claim that a missing customer_id filter always requires a Seq Scan; explain index use conditionally for B-tree.
Describe index use as a cost-dependent possibility, not a guaranteed chosen path; skip scan is a documented example.
Use EXPLAIN to inspect the actual chosen execution plan.

span.text: A multicolumn B-tree index can be used with query conditions that involve any subset of the index's columns, but the index is most efficient when there are constraints on the leading (leftmost) columns.

For example, given an index on (x, y), and a query condition WHERE y = 7700, a B-tree index scan might be able to apply the skip scan optimization. This generally happens when the query planner expects that repeated WHERE x = N AND y = 7700 searches for every possible value of N (or for every x value that is actually stored in the index) is the fastest possible approach, given the available indexes on the table. This approach is generally only taken when there are so few distinct x values that the planner expects the scan to skip over most of the index (because most of its leaf pages cannot possibly contain relevant tuples). If there are many distinct x values, then the entire index will have to be scanned, so in most cases the planner will prefer a sequential table scan over using the index.
You can use the EXPLAIN command to see what query plan the planner creates for any query.

A supported explanation using another valid index-scan path is acceptable; the reference skip-scan example is not a compulsory predicted plan.

questions.question: Is choosing a Seq Scan for a query whose condition matches a partial index necessarily an error?
questions.expected_answer: No. Recognizing that a query condition implies a partial-index predicate makes the index usable, but does not force its selection. A sequential scan can be a sensible cost-based choice, for example for a very small table or a query retrieving common values. Inspect the actual query plan with EXPLAIN rather than treating Seq Scan by itself as evidence of an error.

answer_requirements.statement: Separate recognized predicate implication and index usability from compulsory index selection.
Explain why Seq Scan can be reasonable, using costs, a small table, or common-value access rather than declaring an automatic planner error.

span.text: To be precise, a partial index can be used in a query only if the system can recognize that the WHERE condition of the query mathematically implies the predicate of the index. PostgreSQL does not have a sophisticated theorem prover that can recognize mathematically equivalent expressions that are written in different forms. (Not only is such a general theorem prover extremely difficult to create, it would probably be too slow to be of any real use.) The system can recognize simple inequality implications, for example “x < 1” implies “x < 2”; otherwise the predicate condition must exactly match part of the query's WHERE condition or the index will not be recognized as usable. Matching takes place at query planning time, not at run time.

The planner's cost estimates are not linear and so it might choose a different plan for a larger or smaller table. An extreme example is that on a table that only occupies one disk page, you'll nearly always get a sequential scan plan whether indexes are available or not. The planner realizes that it's going to take one disk page read to process the table in any case, so there's no value in expending additional page reads to look at an index. (We saw this happening in the polygon_tbl example above.)

Normally, PostgreSQL makes reasonable choices about index usage (e.g., it avoids them when retrieving common values, so the earlier example really only saves index size, it is not required to avoid index usage)
You can use the EXPLAIN command to see what query plan the planner creates for any query.

questions.question: Under Read Committed, can two ordinary SELECT statements in the same transaction see different committed data, and why?
questions.expected_answer: Yes. Each ordinary SELECT sees a snapshot as of that query starting. If another transaction commits changes between the two query starts, the second SELECT can see those changes even though both statements are in one transaction.

answer_requirements.statement: Allow successive ordinary SELECT statements in one Read Committed transaction to see different data.
Explain the per-query snapshot and a concurrent commit between query starts.

span.text: Read Committed is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL. When a transaction uses this isolation level, a SELECT query (without a FOR UPDATE/SHARE clause) sees only data committed before the query began; it never sees either uncommitted data or changes committed by concurrent transactions during the query's execution. In effect, a SELECT query sees a snapshot of the database as of the instant the query begins to run. However, SELECT does see the effects of previous updates executed within its own transaction, even though they are not yet committed. Also note that two successive SELECT commands can see different data, even though they are within a single transaction, if other transactions commit changes after the first SELECT starts and before the second SELECT starts.

questions.evidence_combination_note: One passage explicitly states both snapshot timing and the successive-SELECT consequence; no actual transaction observation is claimed.

questions.question: How do ordinary VACUUM and VACUUM FULL differ in returning table space to the operating system, and what table lock does VACUUM FULL require?
questions.expected_answer: Ordinary VACUUM normally makes dead-row space reusable within the table rather than returning it to the operating system. Entirely free pages at the table end are a special exception when an exclusive table lock can be obtained easily. VACUUM FULL writes a compact new table file to shrink the table and return space, requiring an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that prevents concurrent use of that table.

answer_requirements.statement: Distinguish ordinary VACUUM reuse from operating-system space return, preserving the fully free trailing-page exception.
Explain VACUUM FULL as a table rewrite that can shrink the table and return disk space.
Name ACCESS EXCLUSIVE and its incompatibility with concurrent use of the table.

span.text: The standard form of VACUUM removes dead row versions in tables and indexes and marks the space available for future reuse. However, it will not return the space to the operating system, except in the special case where one or more pages at the end of a table become entirely free and an exclusive table lock can be easily obtained. In contrast, VACUUM FULL actively compacts tables by writing a complete new version of the table file with no dead space. This minimizes the size of the table, but can take a long time. It also requires extra disk space for the new copy of the table, until the operation completes.

There are two variants of VACUUM: standard VACUUM and VACUUM FULL. VACUUM FULL can reclaim more disk space but runs much more slowly. Also, the standard form of VACUUM can run in parallel with production database operations. (Commands such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE will continue to function normally, though you will not be able to modify the definition of a table with commands such as ALTER TABLE while it is being vacuumed.) VACUUM FULL requires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the table it is working on, and therefore cannot be done in parallel with other use of the table. Generally, therefore, administrators should strive to use standard VACUUM and avoid VACUUM FULL.

The usual goal of routine vacuuming is to do standard VACUUMs often enough to avoid needing VACUUM FULL. The autovacuum daemon attempts to work this way, and in fact will never issue VACUUM FULL. In this approach, the idea is not to keep tables at their minimum size, but to maintain steady-state usage of disk space: each table occupies space equivalent to its minimum size plus however much space gets used up between vacuum runs. Although VACUUM FULL can be used to shrink a table back to its minimum size and return the disk space to the operating system, there is not much point in this if the table will just grow again in the future. Thus, moderately-frequent standard VACUUM runs are a better approach than infrequent VACUUM FULL runs for maintaining heavily-updated tables.

questions.evidence_combination_note: The selected passages complement space behavior, explicit disk return and locking. They do not establish bytes reclaimed or an observed maintenance outcome.

span.text: It should be noted that a check constraint is satisfied if the check expression evaluates to true or the null value. Since most expressions will evaluate to the null value if any operand is null, they will not prevent null values in the constrained columns. To ensure that a column does not contain null values, the not-null constraint described in the next section can be used.

questions.question: Why can an unresolved x < $1 condition fail to establish the x < 2 predicate of a partial index at query planning time?
questions.expected_answer: Partial-index matching requires a recognized implication at planning time. While $1 is unresolved, x < $1 does not imply x < 2 for every possible parameter value, so that clause alone does not establish the index predicate. This does not claim that every prepared execution is incapable of using a partial index.

answer_requirements.statement: Locate partial-index predicate matching at planning time rather than relying on a later run-time value.
Explain that the unresolved bound does not establish x < 2 for all parameter values, without asserting a universal ban on prepared executions.

span.text: Example 11.2 also illustrates that the indexed column and the column used in the predicate do not need to match. PostgreSQL supports partial indexes with arbitrary predicates, so long as only columns of the table being indexed are involved. However, keep in mind that the predicate must match the conditions used in the queries that are supposed to benefit from the index. To be precise, a partial index can be used in a query only if the system can recognize that the WHERE condition of the query mathematically implies the predicate of the index. PostgreSQL does not have a sophisticated theorem prover that can recognize mathematically equivalent expressions that are written in different forms. (Not only is such a general theorem prover extremely difficult to create, it would probably be too slow to be of any real use.) The system can recognize simple inequality implications, for example “x < 1” implies “x < 2”; otherwise the predicate condition must exactly match part of the query's WHERE condition or the index will not be recognized as usable. Matching takes place at query planning time, not at run time. As a result, parameterized query clauses do not work with a partial index. For example a prepared query with a parameter might specify “x < ?” which will never imply “x < 2” for all possible values of the parameter.

questions.evidence_combination_note: The selected passage explains the planning-time implication problem and its parameterized example. The reference is deliberately scoped to the question's unresolved parameter.

questions.question: Do write_lag, flush_lag and replay_lag in pg_stat_replication predict how long a standby will take to catch up?
questions.expected_answer: No. They measure recent WAL write, flush and replay delays, including the time for the sender to receive notification. They are not predictions of the standby's remaining catch-up time at its current replay rate.

answer_requirements.statement: Describe the fields as measurements of recent WAL processing/notification delays.
Reject interpreting those lag values as a prediction of remaining catch-up time.

span.text: The lag times reported in the pg_stat_replication view are measurements of the time taken for recent WAL to be written, flushed and replayed and for the sender to know about it. These times represent the commit delay that was (or would have been) introduced by each synchronous commit level, if the remote server was configured as a synchronous standby. For an asynchronous standby, the replay_lag column approximates the delay before recent transactions became visible to queries. If the standby server has entirely caught up with the sending server and there is no more WAL activity, the most recently measured lag times will continue to be displayed for a short time and then show NULL.

The reported lag times are not predictions of how long it will take for the standby to catch up with the sending server assuming the current rate of replay. Such a system would show similar times while new WAL is being generated, but would differ when the sender becomes idle. In particular, when the standby has caught up completely, pg_stat_replication shows the time taken to write, flush and replay the most recent reported WAL location rather than zero as some users might expect. This is consistent with the goal of measuring synchronous commit and transaction visibility delays for recent write transactions. To reduce confusion for users expecting a different model of lag, the lag columns revert to NULL after a short time on a fully replayed idle system. Monitoring systems should choose whether to represent this as missing data, zero or continue to display the last known value.

questions.evidence_combination_note: Measurement meaning and the explicit non-prediction warning are complementary. P04 asks about NULL versus zero; this question asks about forecasting, within the same lag-interpretation family.

questions.question: Which transaction profile does Atlas prescribe for a multi-statement reporting export needing one consistent view, and what PostgreSQL snapshot behavior distinguishes it from ordinary Read Committed reporting?
questions.expected_answer: Atlas prescribes read-only Repeatable Read for that export. PostgreSQL uses the snapshot from the transaction's first non-transaction-control statement, so successive SELECTs do not see other transactions' later committed changes. Read Committed instead takes a snapshot for each query, allowing a later SELECT to see commits between query starts. This is the intended Atlas profile, not an observation of a live session's configuration.

answer_requirements.statement: Identify the Atlas export profile as read-only Repeatable Read.
Explain the snapshot fixed at the first non-transaction-control statement and the stable view across successive SELECTs.
Contrast Read Committed's per-query snapshot and visibility of commits between query starts.

span.text:
Workload	Intended transaction profile
Routine single-statement reporting	Read-only, Read Committed
Multi-statement reporting export requiring one consistent view	Read-only, Repeatable Read
Application order creation	Serializable on the primary

This level is different from Read Committed in that a query in a repeatable read transaction sees a snapshot as of the start of the first non-transaction-control statement in the transaction, not as of the start of the current statement within the transaction. Thus, successive SELECT commands within a single transaction see the same data, i.e., they do not see changes made by other transactions that committed after their own transaction started.

Read Committed is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL. When a transaction uses this isolation level, a SELECT query (without a FOR UPDATE/SHARE clause) sees only data committed before the query began; it never sees either uncommitted data or changes committed by concurrent transactions during the query's execution. In effect, a SELECT query sees a snapshot of the database as of the instant the query begins to run. However, SELECT does see the effects of previous updates executed within its own transaction, even though they are not yet committed. Also note that two successive SELECT commands can see different data, even though they are within a single transaction, if other transactions commit changes after the first SELECT starts and before the second SELECT starts.

questions.evidence_combination_note: Atlas supplies the workload-specific profile; PostgreSQL explains its snapshot semantics and contrast with Read Committed. The family is shared with P22; this is a distinct policy/application question, not another independent held-out case.
